Sure, and I might tap my colleague behind me. Um, so I think the first point is that these pro— these, uh, projects will all remain

subject to any of our, uh, normal enforcement programs. So should there be concerns and complaints, we will be responsive to those. We will also, as we've talked about, conduct a roof-to-cellar inspection. Um, uh, however, what I wanna flag is that there might be difficulties at different points in accessing the property as it's moving its way through this process. We're aware of that as a limiting factor and so we just wanna make sure, um, that we're, ah, cautious about that, but also, ah, all of the normal, ah, processes and tools that HPD has at hand will continue to be part of our toolkit.

Thank you. Um, and finally, for now, for HPD, at this Committee's hearing a few years ago, you testified that 62 properties were transferred in Round 10. Can you just give us an update on these 62 properties?

Sure, thank you for that question. I'm happy to speak to that. Um, 64 properties, uh, eventually have been transferred to Neighborhood Restore as our interim owner. Um, that number increased because of resolution of some litigation post that initial 28-round. 43 of those properties

have been transferred to a third party, and 21 properties remain with Neighborhood Restore. Of the 43, uh, 16 have completed construction, and the remaining 27 are mid-construction.
So the 21 properties that are still with Neighborhood Restore, can you describe to us why they are still with Neighborhood Restore?

Sure, 6 of those are vacant lots, um, 15 are buildings. 4 of those buildings are in litigation. The remainder of the buildings have designated, um, entities, and we're working through the pre-development process.
How many vacant lots?
Uh, 6.

6, Got it thank you. All right, Um, you know, a, a very important part of this conversation is just making sure that we— er, our processes are as strong as they can be. So just turning to the outreach, um, and what information agencies have in order to do that outreach. Can you talk— can each agency talk about what information or how good your information is for property owners? A couple years ago, HPD testified that you rely heavily on the multiple dwelling registration. Has

that process moved online? Are you seeing higher rates of compliance? Um, DEP testified that you relied heavily on the registered to, um, the ratepayers who are registered to my DEP? Have the numbers, uh, increased for those registrations? And for the Department of Finance, you said you, uh, rely heavily on mail, um, and you don't require email or phone in most interactions. Has, has that changed?

Um, we encourage our customers, taxpayers to give us their email address, their cell phone, um, at, at the time they interact with us. We have changed all our forms for all our different type of, um, applications, whether it's an exemption or something in another area that's not dealing with, um, the exemption unit, to have email addresses and phone numbers. Um, again, it ends up being up to the customer to give us that information, but we do encourage it, and it is asked on every application. As of now, we have about 45,000 email addresses— I'm sorry, 55,000 email addresses and about 45,000 cell phone numbers, but it's encouraged at intervals when we talk to customers to give us that information.
Out of how many properties? This is just residential or this is across?
This is across the board.
So, across 1 million properties in the City of New York, you have 55,000 email addresses?
Yes again, we encourage— we encourage the customers to give it to us, but it's up to them to, um, give it as we, um, deal with them.

And so for these 55,000 email addresses and 45,000 cell phone numbers, what is, uh, the Department of Finance's, uh, sort of protocol for redundancy? Are you - are you emailing every notice that you mail, or are you only emailing— what, what do you use email for versus what you're mailing?

Well, customers have to, um, have to opt in to get emails. It's just not necessarily we just send the emails out to them, um, but we will email notification and notices. They write in from, ah, um, a billing problem, we'll email them. If they give us the email address through our, um, our, um, system we use for dealing with, um, correspondence

and questions. If they write in, we'll email them back that information. Again, if we have it and it's a— and they want it to be emailed, we'll email it back to them but they have to opt in for email.
So for property tax bills, for, um, delinquencies, are you mailing and emailing when you have contact information that is broader?
Yes.
And what about for— now I'm just being s— like, things like you, uh, that you mail, like the notice of property value, are you also emailing that?
Uh, let me just double-check with my Counsel. We're not emailing the notice of property value.
And why not? Is it an opt-in problem?
State law limits how we, um, we have to send it through the mail. State law limits that action.
State law says you can't email? Yes. Uh, in this case. Okay. Um, okay, thank you.
I could get back to you. We'll double-check to make sure, but as of now, it's state law, and that's it but let's get back to you on that to be sure.

So HPD has a multiple dwelling registration requirement for properties that are 3, uh, units and above. One, you know, my, my original question is, um, what is compliance with that registration requirement look like? You know, what is the rate that we're seeing for the 700,000-ish properties that we have, residential properties we have in the City of New York, and why isn't, why isn't there data sharing? Because 55,000 emails sounds like there's not data sharing.

Thank you, Council Member. Uh, so not every property that is DOF is required— thank you— is required to register with HPD. Right now we have a pool of about 170,000 properties that are required to register with us, and that includes all multiple dwellings, right, 3 units or more, and then, uh, 1 or 2-family dwellings if the— neither the owner nor their relative lives in the property, right? So it's a significant difference. Um, of our 170,000, uh, properties, uh, we also have about

50,000, 45,000 emails. That covers about 100,000 properties, though. So obviously some people are registered for more than one property. Um, we use that information right now to, uh, email owners about complaints we receive and violations that are issued. It's not the official notification because, uh, we'd love to talk to you about that, too, in the future, but, uh, separate conversation. Um, uh, property registration still requires a hard copy signature for us at this point. Uh, again, potentially a, a conversation for another day. Um, but most large properties are registered, so it's upwards of 90% of, of bigger properties in the city that are registered. We do have challenges registering small properties, 3, 4, 5-unit properties, and we continue to work on increasing that percentage. Perhaps simplifying some of the requirements would assist us to increase that percentage.
Got it. Um, for— did you say that property registration requires, uh, that has to be sent in via snail mail?
Yes, I did.
Yeah, I saw that last night. Um, not, not good. Let's, uh, can we change that in the city? Is that city statute, or—
We would be happy to continue that conversation, Council Member.

Great, okay we'll LS it right now. Um, so there, there notwithstanding, there are penalties associated with not registering with the City of New York. I see subject, um, any, anyone who fails to file as required shall be subject to civil penalties between $500 and $1,500 for multiple dwelling with 5 units or less. There's a lot of thousands of dollars, uh, in, in this, uh, block of text here. How often is HPD issuing those violations for those 70,000 properties that you said you don't have?
Oh, we do issue violations every year once the period passes for registration. Um, we do not often seek civil penalties. Again, most of those properties that fail to register are smaller properties.

For the universe that we're talking about, um, focusing the new— the new program on, the SAFER Act on, um, are you— how is your

coverage of contact information in terms of cell phones, emails, and addresses for these properties?

Again, this is a sample of the 200 and 500, but as the properties get larger, as it goes from 10 units to 30 units, should we go to the critical eligible definition, I think we will have, you know, anecdotally we will have good coverage of those properties.
Including HDFC co-ops?
HDFC co-ops are required to register.

Thank you. And so moving, moving to DEP and ratepayers, um, there's this one example somewhere in my notes of just a misadminister— misadministration of, um, a tax— not a tax lien, a water lien that was misapplied and a property was transferred and then, and then it was reversed. Um, but how, how is uptake with my, my DEP looking in 2026?

Absolutely, and Council Member, uh, thank you for the opportunity to, to be here and if I could just introduce myself, my name is Albert Kramer, the Deputy Commissioner for the Bureau of Customer Services. Um, and I also want to say that we

at DEP, um, are very supportive of TPT, um, the public policy goal of helping tenants and to enforce property taxes in a fair and equitable manner. Um, so in terms of my DEP account uptake, we have, uh, approximately 540,000 of our 8,038,000 customers that are enrolled. Um, that means for all of those customers, we have email addresses. And just to sort of, uh, go to the question before, before addressing your, your current question, um, I think the outreach and partnership that happened between DOF, HPD, and the Mayor's Office for the FY25 lien sale is a great model where DEP had email addresses and actually very effectively we had cell phone numbers for a lot of the folks that were on the lean sale list. So for the first time, we shared those with our agency partners so they could do text message outreach, emails. So I think there's opportunities to model that here for third-party transfer if and when the program were to move ahead so we take a city approach towards outreach as opposed to those, ah, silos. And in terms of your question, I believe you're referring to a situation in which a payment was applied to the wrong account. And so the, ah,

customer that was making the payment, we're reliant on them to tell us which account number they wanted to be applied to. Um, the fact that it was for a TPT-type eligible property that went down this path is a, a rare but ultimately unfortunate type of situation. And I can just assure you that, you know, going forward, uh, for a new population of TPT, um, we would be manually reviewing these types of, uh, accounts. We would be tracking whether payments have come in. Um, and we would certainly do outbound research and outreach to customers to ensure that, you know, if they say, hey, I paid— I thought I paid that bill, um, you know, we'll make sure that we take that seriously, uh, to track that down or to help ensure that they understand, uh, how much they owe.

Thank you. That's, that's great to hear about the, um, the sharing of information and, you know, one of, one of the goals that we have in this, uh, overhaul is to inform more entities, more people, more, more folks about what is happening. Um, I think it's a wonderful and a great start to have DEP share information with finance and HPD,

maybe even just beyond, uh, this program, but just in general, there should be some sharing. Um, but what about, um, our goal of sharing information with tenants, with additional shareholders, with, um, with more of the folks that if they had, uh, some sort of early alarm, uh, that their, their property was subject to transfer, the per— or the place where they lived was subject to transfer, that might activate further action. Um, what, what does HPD, uh, have on that? And in, in the case of DEP and DOF, for DEP, are there ratepayers that are not the primary owner, um, where you have information that you could share with HPD? And similarly with DOF, do you have other sources of information that could, uh, supplement HPD's information?

Thank you. We're, we're happy to share any information we have of property with our partners at HPD. We do, based on our tax bills, sometimes we do get in where there's a third party who, who is aware of the property, who might pay for the, the, um, bill, or who wants to be on the property records. Those information can be shared with our partners at any time.
But you don't— you’re just happy to moving forward? Have you had conversations?

Right now we do share information with DP about ownership. I'm not sure if what prop— what information that they might not be getting, but we could definitely take a look at it to make sure that they're getting all the ownership information that we have.

Thank you. I mean, and, and what I have in, uh, in mind here is if Department of Finance has folks that are registered for SCRIE or DRIE or, you know, er, any of these exemptions that are tied to an address, ah, for a property that is going through the new version of Safer Homes, um, that information can be used to contact those folks and alert them that changes.

Yes, yes, I understand but that's the same thing as we have people who also registered to pay the tax bill that's related to, like, a child paying for the parent. We could share that information also because we do have, um, the, the names on the record.
Thank you.
Thank you.

Um, I can speak to the question about, um, notifications of shareholders and residents. Um, we agree that additional outreach and notifications are necessary and support that, um, in terms of the, the proposed legislation. Um, in terms of what we are, we are recommending is, uh, I think kind of two different types of notifications. One, before the action commences, we'll be providing additional notices. Um, as I mentioned earlier, these early notices will go to the HDFC co-ops as well as all of the building owners um, where their properties may be vulnerable to in rem foreclosure. We're also adding to the statute an additional notice that will be posted within the building and the building common areas where we're able to get access, so tenants and shareholders are aware shortly after the action commences that the building is at risk of in rem foreclosure.

So just, just to clarify, so notice posted within buildings, sure, that's— it's very clear how, you know, residents would be able to see that. The, the first early notice that you mentioned, what— how is— what's the mechanism for shareholders

and tenants or residents to see that who are not on the board, or if it's a co-op?

Um, one of the things that we have to balance, um, in terms of our notification is the timing and the milestones, um, where alerting owners, shareholder board, or the building owner versus the tenants and shareholders has to be balanced with that information. So the early warning notice that I mentioned would go to the building owner, so whoever is, is registered and receiving those notifications pre-commencement. After the action commences and the building is getting, you know, further along in the interim foreclosure process, that is when we would alert, um, tenants and shareholders in a building.
Directly or through these hallway postings?
Through the postings.

Okay, so just— I, I sat through as a, as a, um, you know, humble staffer many hearings where HPD talked about posting in, in corridors and posting by elevators that tenants never saw, that residents never saw.

So I just take my skepticism that they will see it moving forward. I, I continue to be concerned about that and want to ensure that we land on a mechanism that has this information going before all shareholders' eyes and residents' eyes.
We're happy to keep discussing.

Thank you. Um, okay, last, last, uh, question here for, for DEP, unless somebody flags for me that I didn't— I committed an egregious error in not asking something. Um, but on, on DEP's charges, and, and again going back to, you know, the primary goal that all properties are stable, everybody is in good condition. Um, can you talk about the, the rates of disputes of water and sewer charges? Um, how many ratepayers in, say, the last fiscal year or two dispute— disputed water and sewer charges with DEP? And how do you help, um, how do you help New Yorkers with, say, leak protection, right? Uh, if, if folks have a leak, then they might see a doubling or tripling of their bill, um, and how does DEP help New Yorkers with that?

Absolutely, so I'll start with the last, uh, part of your question. So we, we offer

something called our Leak Notification Program, which is that we, we have water meters and then we have a smart reader that's communicating the readings associated with that water meter and if we notice, um, a large spike in consumption, um, we have an algorithm in place to flag that for, for customers. To let them know that they may need to— you'd be amazed how much a running toilet, um, can lead to an increase in one's water bill. Um, and so we're trying as best as we can to proactively communicate that. And then as a part of those proactive communications, even if after fixing the leak, the customer may see that their bill has increased, um, as a result of that leak, and then we offer something we call the Leak Forgiveness Program, uh, which customers can dispute their bill or essentially apply for that program that applies- that um, provides relief up to 50% of the, uh, the, the increase in their bill due to their leak. Um, Council Member, I don't have on hand specific dispute, um, stats about like the last calendar fiscal year, but I will provide that as a follow-up. Um, but what I will say, and this is something that's very important to DEP, um, as part of all of our

enforcement processes, is, you know, we— if we make a mistake or there's something off without a dispute, we fix it. Um, and then when it comes to lien sale or third-party transfer or any other enforcement, um, process such as service terminations, you know, as a matter of practice, we ensure that we review those disputes, uh, before a determine is made— determination is made. If we don't feel that we can fully do that review in the timeline we have, we'll remove that property, uh, from that enforcement process, um, to really ensure that that property goes through and is able to exercise their full dispute rights.

Thank you. That's helpful to understand and similarly, Department of Finance, um, especially in light of reforms that came through the lien sale reforms that we undertook in the Council. If a homeowner has outstanding property tax debt today, what, what is, uh, what is DOF putting on the table to assist these homeowners?

We have several, um, several, um, different type of payment plans that customers could, um, enter into for, um, to be removed from the lien sale.

We also, as, uh, my partner in DEP has said, if there is an issue with trying to determine, um, there's a problem with, with the payment, we will remove any issues or any type of, um, research that needs to be done. We'll remove that property from the lien sale to ensure that it's not sold hold, um, until we've resolved the issue. We also have, as, um, Council, um, through the Legislative Council, we have the easy exit removal, which worked very well, where it gives up to 3 times a person could be requested to remove from the lien sale, um, with no, no questions. So just come to us, fill out the form. We, we put this in place last year at the 2025 lien sale, which worked very well. We also have done, um, extensive outreach, which have really helped during this last lean sale, where we were able to tell the, um, customers the different off-ramps they have to be removed from the lean sale. Um, there was a new circuit breaker, PTA circuit breaker, um, installment agreement that was implemented, um, as well as our standard agreements and all of their different exemptions at each outreach session and every billing.

We also mention every single outreach that— I mean, exemptions that people could possibly qualify for.

Could you repeat just the beginning of the question?
Wouldn't these vacant properties, these vacant buildings that are—

The latest AEP report. The year ‘17 report, not the round '17 report.

If they don't meet the criteria, they would be subject to any of the other enforcement programs or remain in AEP. You know, I think this gets back to a little bit of, uh, some of what we were discussing with Council Member Epstein, sort of that sort of balance of, of having that objective criteria. Okay, thank you. Just reviewing my notes here. What were these— where— what are these buildings, um, what were the conditions there? Were these build— were these properties known to the city? I've asked these questions for a month now, and I have not received a response. Uh, so if you have anything, please share. Uh, but, uh, I did receive responses last night that told me nothing, uh, from City Hall and I, I just implore the Administration to share this information with the public so that we can make better decisions moving forward.

since 1843, uh, and we have been at the forefront of advocacy for better housing conditions since the beginning, from the city's first tenement laws in the 1800s to contemporary organizing for strong tenants' rights. would improve TPT, um, its targeting, and increase outreach to building owners. Good afternoon, Council Member. I'm Russell Crane, I'm a staff attorney at the Legal Aid Society's Housing Justice Unit, Advocacy Unit. Uh, it's great to be here today, um, uh, in front of you. Uh, to begin with, uh, want to just express, uh, deep thanks for your advocacy and leadership, uh, with regard to your, your constituents and, and our clients at, uh, 2201 O5 Davidson. Um, and, uh, wanted to talk about, uh, that building, uh, because it shows the importance of the legislative, uh, before you, the Safer Homes Act.

So 2201 05 Davidson is a 49-unit rent-stabilized building in the University Heights neighborhood in the Bronx. And it's— it is an example of, uh, what happens when, uh, there's a building that remains in limbo, uh, for a long period of time from a neglectful owner. Um, and, and what can happen when that, that exists for a long time. So 2201 Davidson had experienced neglect many years ago. Um, in 2015, the city, uh, had placed 2201 Davidson into round 10 of the TPT program, um, because there were already millions of dollars in property tax debt, uh, in deplorable conditions in the building. Uh, the people who then took control of the, uh, the LLC owner of the building, managed to stop the TPT program through a federal bankruptcy filing. Um, but after doing that, it became clear that they had no plan to, uh, to resolve this property tax debt owed to the city and to address the conditions. Um, so because of the, the bankruptcy filing, it stopped the TPT transfer process. The city, uh, and the tenants, um, asked the bankruptcy court to dismiss the case because the owners didn't do

anything in bankruptcy court to resolve the property tax debt with the city. It was finally dismissed from bankruptcy court in 2018, uh, and had the TBT program been functioning then, the building could have proceeded into the TBT transfer process without the building conditions, uh, worsening, which has happened over, uh, the preceding 8 years. Um, so they, at that time then, the Davidson tenants, uh, found themselves in this world where, uh, there was an owner that had no plan, long-term plan to resolve the debt, no long-term plan for repairs, uh, but there was no— nothing the city, uh, had available at the time because of the, the legal complications with the existing TPT program. Um, and so it was I mean, the— it was deeply difficult, uh, for tenants who are living at the building. And, um, I wanna say also our organizing partners, uh, from Northwest Bronx, our, our Bronx are, are also here and, uh, one of the tenants from Davidson who you may, uh, hear from in, in just a bit about what it was like. But I mean, the elevator stopped working for, for 2 years at the, er, at the end. Um, leaving people having to walk 6 flights, uh,

mentioned, uh, leaks, um, and, and vermin infestations. So deplorable conditions. Uh, the owner completely stopped even cleaning common areas of the building, so tenants had to come together themselves to pool funds, uh, to, to do cleaning. Uh, another aspect that, that I think is com— happened in Davidson is common in these buildings is that because the owner was leaving the building, the, the front door lock was broken. So trespassers would enter and Davidson tenants felt threatened by people who would come into their building who shouldn't have been there. Um, but ultimately because of tenants' advocacy, ah, and, ah, and, and, and with your support, the building was finally able to be moved into the TPT transfer program, but I think it it stands as an example of, um, where, um, you know, had it been able to happen earlier, some of the conditions that now will cost more and take longer to fix could have been, could have been addressed earlier.

Thank you and I, and I know I, I'm supposed to cut, cut folks off at the 2-minute mark, but I know that there were so many years that you were working on this case, and I just want to

personally again thank you for, for that work with 2201 Davidson, because we wouldn't be be here, uh, without that and the work of Northwest Bronx. Thank you.

Uh, thank you, Council Member, for the opportunity to testify. We appreciate the Council's continued leadership in strengthening tools that address distressed housing while preserving affordability and housing stability. Um, sorry I didn't introduce myself. I'm Robert Dazier of the Legal Aid Society Civil Law Reform Unit, and we're very thankful for your leadership in bringing this legislation and the work that you have done with our, um, clients in the Bronx. Um, first, this legislation is necessary because traditional enforcement tools often fail when buildings fall into severe financial and physical distress. The Legal Aid Society's economic equities and group advocacy projects regularly work with tenants and small homeowners facing these conditions. During these periods where ownership has effectively walked away or lacks capacity to maintain the property, tenants stay in place while essential services fail.

The TPT program is critical because it provides a mechanism not just to enforce violations but to transfer distressed buildings to responsible ownership capable of rehabilitating them and maintaining safe affordable housing. Secondly, Intro 657 strengthens protections for the tenants who are left behind in these distressed buildings. The bill promotes earlier intervention and clearer enforcement standards so that buildings experiencing severe deterioration can be addressed sooner. It also improves transparency and communication. For tenants, this means a greater likelihood that longstanding hazardous conditions will be addressed and that their homes will remain affordable and secure during and after ownership transitions. At the same time, this legislation appropriately incorporates protections for small homeowners. Finally, the success of this legislation will depend on strong implementation. Tenant participation in issues such as management selection and major rehabilitation decisions must remain central. Strong oversight of successor sponsors is also essential to ensure that repairs are completed and buildings move

toward long-term stability. The program must be supported with adequate financial and technical resources, including training and support for buildings transitioning to cooperative or nonprofit ownership models. Again, we thank you for the opportunity to testify. Our written testimony will be submitted shortly. Um, we look forward to any questions.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, Chair Sanchez, and thank you for holding this hearing today. Uh, my name is Lacey Tauber. I'm representing Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso. Who wants to thank you and your team for giving this legislation the time, attention, and thoughtfulness required for it to be successful. Uh, since 1996, the TPT program has been an important tool in the city's toolbox to hold landlords accountable, protect tenants, and preserve and improve affordable housing. Its goal is to transfer properties with high municipal debt and poor living conditions from delinquent landlords to responsible owners. However, the program's existing enabling legislation contains multiple issues that

caused too many properties, including owner-occupied homes, to be swept up in the last round. This led to unnecessary foreclosures and lawsuits and undermined the program's purpose. The SAFER Homes Act addresses these issues and creates the framework for a more targeted program that focuses on the most distressed properties, those with the highest levels of debt and hazardous or immediately hazardous violations.
